Dermatology · published research

Contact dermatitis

Two animal studies report reduced inflammation in selected allergic contact dermatitis models, while an irritant-dermatitis model did not improve. The results vary with treatment timing, and there is no clinical evidence in people with contact dermatitis.

Evidence summary

What the evidence suggests

Two mouse studies report reduced inflammation in selected allergic contact dermatitis models, but an irritant model did not improve and treatment just after challenge could worsen swelling. The evidence is preclinical, with no treatment study in people.

Summary of the Evidence

Two mouse experiments report reduced inflammatory responses in selected allergic contact dermatitis settings. The older study found no benefit in irritant dermatitis and showed that the direction of the response depended on timing. Laboratory assays in the same papers add mechanistic observations but do not provide independent replications.

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical PBM treatment study in people with allergic or irritant contact dermatitis was identified in the directly relevant records.

Animal evidence

In mice, Sakihama tested helium-neon laser exposure around the time of a dermatitis challenge. Irradiation before the challenge reduced swelling in the allergic model, while the irritant model did not improve. Irradiation five minutes after challenge increased swelling, showing that timing changed the observed response (Sakihama 1995).

Fu et al. reported lower inflammatory response and fewer T cells after PBM in a C57BL/6 mouse model of allergic contact dermatitis. The study also tested isolated naïve T cells in vitro and linked reduced activation to TGF-β signaling (Fu et al. 2024).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

In the same Fu et al. paper, an isolated naïve T-cell assay found moderated activation associated with TGF-β signaling (Fu et al. 2024). Sakihama’s ex-vivo rat mast-cell assay found that selected exposures reduced spontaneous histamine release, while substance P- and compound 48/80-induced release was not reduced. These laboratory assays are parts of the two animal-study publications, not additional independent trials (Sakihama 1995).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Sakihama used a continuous-wave 632.8-nm helium-neon laser at 12.2 J/cm² for the mouse-ear experiments. Irradiation was tested at several times before and after challenge; the five-minute post-challenge exposure increased swelling. The mast-cell experiments tested 6.24, 12.48, and 18.72 J/cm², with effects depending on the trigger (Sakihama 1995).

The accessible report of the newer mouse study does not provide enough wavelength, dose, or schedule detail to compare its settings with the earlier experiment (Fu et al. 2024). No human dose-finding or clinical treatment schedule is available.

Interpretation

The findings support a possible timing- and model-specific effect in allergic contact dermatitis. They do not show that PBM improves contact dermatitis in patients, and the irritant-model and post-challenge results caution against generalizing the favorable findings across dermatitis types or schedules.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low for changes in experimental allergic contact dermatitis. Results come from two mouse studies with different models and timing, and no patient treatment study is available.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Both directly relevant publications are preclinical. The 1995 mouse study found different results for allergic and irritant dermatitis, and irradiation shortly after challenge increased swelling. The newer mouse report adds an allergic model and cell findings, but does not provide sufficient accessible dose details to compare protocols. There are no human clinical outcomes (Sakihama 1995; Fu et al. 2024).
